food.text: Mrs Rundell's A New System of Domestic Cookery, published in 1806, helped bring systematic cooking to the English middle classes. It went through sixty-seven editions by 1844, selling hundreds of thousands of copies in Britain and America.
tags: A New System of Domestic Cookery

food.text: Chocolate bars were developed and marketed in England by three Quaker-founded businesses. Joseph Fry's came first in 1847, then Rowntree's in 1862 and Cadbury's in 1868.

Georges Auguste Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire, published in 1903, established the fundamentals of French cookery. It moved away from heavy sauces toward lighter fumets, using sauces and garnishes to add to a dish's flavor rather than mask it.

The modern version of French onion soup dates from the mid-19th century, in Les Halles, the large food and flower market in Paris. Restaurants around the market, including La Poule au Pot, Chez Baratte and Au Pied de Cochon, served it topped with grated cheese and put under a grill.
Eliza Acton's Modern Cookery for Private Families appeared in 1845. Bee Wilson has called it "the greatest cookery book in our language", though it was "modern" only in a nineteenth-century sense.

Escoffier also simplified and organized the modern menu and structure of the meal, and published his Livre des menus in 1912. His approach embraced the service à la russe, serving meals in separate courses on individual plates, which Félix Urbain Dubois had made popular in the 1860s.

The first Indian restaurant in England, the Hindoostane Coffee House, opened in London around 1810. It offered curries and a hookah-smoking room, and its founder, Sake Dean Mohomed, stated that the ingredients were authentically Indian.

Around 1810 the Hindoostane Coffee House opened in London, the first Indian restaurant in England. It offered curries and a hookah-smoking room. Its founder, Sake Dean Mohomed, said the curry ingredients and smoking herbs were authentically Indian, and The Epicure's Almanack in 1815 noted the dishes used curry powder, rice, Cayenne and spices.
Tea had once been too expensive for most people in England, since its cost restricted it to wealthy consumers. Its price gradually dropped, until by the 19th century its use was widespread.

Sugar was entirely imported into Britain until around 1900 and the growing of sugar beet. James Walvin argues that sugar, tea, coffee, potatoes and spices were "Fruits of Empire", and by the nineteenth century their exotic origins had been forgotten.

Marie-Antoine Carême's writings, in which soufflés appear for the first time, simplified and codified an even more complex cuisine that existed before him. Central to this were Le Maître d'hôtel français (1822), Le Cuisinier parisien (1828) and L'Art de la cuisine française au dix-neuvième siècle (1833–5).

A recipe for soupe à l'oignon was printed in Britain in The Cook and Housewife's Manual, published in Edinburgh in 1826. It resembled the modern version, with onions gently cooked and then simmered in veal stock. Some 1880s British recipes called "French onion soup" used milk or water thickened with flour and had no cheese.

In the mid-19th century, vendors in London sold warm elderberry wine to laborers. At the end of the century, warmed elderberry wine was the most popular Christmas drink in Surrey, and in Devon large demand sustained a large elderberry industry.

art.text: Two English Romantics, John Constable and J. M. W. Turner, are largely credited with raising the status of landscape painting worldwide. Turner in particular is credited with elevating landscape painting to an eminence rivalling history painting.

Walter Benjamin called Paris "the capital of the 19th century". Café culture, cabarets, arcades, anarchism, the mixing of classes and a boisterous willingness to shock all made for a stunning artistic vibrancy, which the article calls the birth of Modernism.

Romanticism in early 19th-century France set up a debate between the proponents of line, exemplified by Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres, and those favoring violent colors and curves, like Eugène Delacroix. The article calls the comparison somewhat false, because Ingres' intense realism sometimes gives way to amazing voluptuousness in his orientalised bath scenes. Romanticism departed from classicism, embracing Orientalism, tragic anti-heroes, wild landscapes and themes from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.

Impressionist painters such as Claude Monet captured transient light effects outdoors, inspired partly by J.M.W. Turner. Some of their techniques were made possible by new paints available in tubes, and they were also in dialogue with the new invention of photography.

In England, the Gothic Revival gained backing from the Oxford Movement in the second quarter of the 19th century. The period of its widest appeal, 1855 to 1885, is known in Britain as High Victorian Gothic.

The Palace of Westminster in London was designed by Sir Charles Barry, with interiors by Augustus Welby Pugin, a major exponent of the early Gothic Revival. Later examples include George Gilbert Scott's Albert Memorial and William Butterfield's chapel at Keble College, Oxford.

Around 1800, Greek Revival architecture brought sobriety and restraint to British public buildings, as an assertion of nationalism. William Wilkins's winning design for Downing College, Cambridge announced that the Greek style would be dominant. He and Robert Smirke went on to build the British Museum, the General Post Office and the National Gallery.

Édouard Manet's work bridged 19th-century art with modernism and led the way to Impressionism. His rediscovery of Spanish painting, his willingness to show the unpainted canvas, his exploration of the forthright nude and his radical brush strokes were the first step toward it. Claude Monet and his contemporaries advanced the movement by capturing transient light effects outdoors, inspired partly by J.M.W. Turner and the advent of paint in tubes.

Édouard Manet's work bridged 19th-century art with modernism and led the way to Impressionism, partly through his exploration of the forthright nude. His era saw Paris reshaped by Haussmannization, which replaced poorer neighborhoods and created fast routes to move troops through the city to quell unrest. The Paris of this time was also marked by a blend of social classes and radical art movements.

John Linnell was a rival to Constable in his time, and Paul Sandby is recognised as the father of English watercolour painting. Thomas Girtin, Turner's friend, was one of the watercolourists who followed.

The British Museum needed a major extension after the 1822 donation of the King's Library, which held some 120,000 manuscripts, pamphlets and drawings. Robert Smirke's Greek Revival building replaced Montagu House. Its Round Reading Room had the second largest dome in the world when finished, at 140 feet in diameter.

The early 19th century saw the emergence of the Norwich school of painters, the first provincial art movement outside of London. Its members included John Crome (1768–1821), John Sell Cotman (1782–1842), James Stark and Joseph Stannard.

The gallant spirit of 19th century English military art helped shape Victorian England's self-image. Thomas Davidson, who specialised in historical naval scenes, included reproductions of Nelson-related works by Arnald, Westall and Abbott in England's Pride and Glory (1894).

In Scotland, Thomas Hamilton worked with the artists Andrew Wilson and Hugh William Williams on monuments and buildings of international significance. They include the Burns Monument at Alloway (1818) and the Royal High School, Edinburgh (1823 to 1829).

war.text: In July 1870 the Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck provoked Napoleon into declaring war on Prussia. The French troops were swiftly defeated in the following weeks, and on September 1 the main army, with the emperor himself, was trapped at Sedan and forced to surrender. A republic was quickly proclaimed in Paris, but the war was far from over.
war.source_title: France in the long nineteenth century

war.text: The Prussians laid siege to Paris, and new armies mustered by France failed to alter this situation. The French capital began experiencing severe food shortages, to the extent that even the animals in the zoo were eaten.
war.source_title: France in the long nineteenth century

war.text: As the city of Paris was being bombarded by Prussian siege guns in January 1871, King William of Prussia was proclaimed Emperor of Germany in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Shortly afterwards, on January 28, 1871, Paris surrendered.
war.source_title: France in the long nineteenth century

war.text: The peace treaty after the Franco-Prussian War was harsh. France ceded Alsace and Lorraine to Germany and had to pay an indemnity of 5 billion francs, with German troops staying in the country until it was paid. The fallen Napoleon III went into exile in England, where he died in 1873.
war.source_title: France in the long nineteenth century

war.text: France's conflicts with China over Indochina climaxed in the Sino-French War of 1884 to 1885, when Admiral Courbet destroyed the Chinese fleet anchored at Foochow. The treaty gave France a protectorate over northern and central Vietnam, which it divided into Tonkin and Annam.
war.source_title: France in the long nineteenth century

war.text: Despite its defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, France was still considered a military example. A second French military mission to Japan (1872 to 1880) built the Ichigaya Military Academy in 1874. In 1877 the modernized Imperial Japanese Army defeated the Satsuma rebellion led by Saigō Takamori.

Japan's Bakufu modernized its army with the help of French military missions, including Jules Brunet. Japan later relied on France for the early shipbuilding industry of its Imperial Japanese Navy, associated with Emile Bertin.

literature.text: Among the early Romantics were the Lake Poets, a small group of friends including William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Robert Southey and the journalist Thomas De Quincey. Yet at the time, Walter Scott was the most famous poet of all.

Charles Dickens emerged on the literary scene in the late 1830s and soon became probably the most famous novelist in the history of British literature. He fiercely satirised society, attacking the workhouse in Oliver Twist and the failures of the legal system in Bleak House.

The immense popularity of Victor Hugo's novel Notre Dame de Paris fed a movement to restore the cathedral. In 1837 a commission of Historic Monuments was created, headed by Prosper Mérimée, himself the author of popular novellas. Between 1845 and 1850 the battered cathedral, which had been semi-ruined and stripped of its decoration, was restored.

William Le Queux's novel The Great War in England in 1897, published in 1894, shows Britain invaded by a coalition led by France and Russia, who make several early advances. The English patriots fight on and turn the tide, especially once Germany enters the war on the British side. The invasion then goes the other way: the victors divide the spoils, Britain seizes Algeria and Russian Central Asia, Germany annexes more of mainland France, and the enemies are left crushed. The book was a huge success and went through eight editions.
literature.source_title: The Great War in England in 1897
tags: The Great War in England in 1897

literature.text: Walter Scott achieved immediate success with his long narrative poem The Lay of the Last Minstrel in 1805. He followed it with the full epic poem Marmion in 1808. Both were set in the distant Scottish past.
tags: The Lay of the Last Minstrel

literature.text: Robert Browning's great innovation was the dramatic monologue, which he used to the full in The Ring and the Book, a long novel in verse. His wife Elizabeth Barrett Browning is best remembered for Sonnets from the Portuguese, while her long poem Aurora Leigh is a classic of 19th century feminist literature.

In 1802 François-René de Chateaubriand, aged thirty-four, published The Genius of Christianity. After its success, Napoleon named him secretary of his Embassy in Rome. He had another literary success in 1809 with his novel Les Martyrs.

Romanticism in France defied political affiliation. Its writers included liberal strains like Stendhal, conservative ones like Chateaubriand, and socialist ones like George Sand, whose peasant stories affirmed the common man and the natural setting.

The Condition-of-England question was a Victorian debate over the English working class during the Industrial Revolution. Thomas Carlyle first proposed it in his essay Chartism in 1839, asking what the bitter discontent of the Working Classes meant and on what terms it would depart.

Invasion literature began with The Battle of Dorking in 1871, in which the British are soundly defeated by an invading German army. George Chesney wrote it as a warning against further demobilisation of the British armed forces.
literature.source_title: The Great War in England in 1897

literature.text: Dante Gabriel Rossetti belonged to the inner circle of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood and was a poet of some ability. His sister Christina Rossetti is generally considered the greater poet. Their verse shared an interest in Medieval models and an almost obsessive attention to visual detail.

In 1884 Paul Verlaine used the phrase poète maudit, meaning accursed poet, for poets like Tristan Corbière, Stéphane Mallarmé and Arthur Rimbaud. They had fought against poetic conventions and suffered social rebuke or been ignored by critics. With Jean Moréas's Symbolist Manifesto in 1886, the term symbolism became the most common label.

Le Queux's scenario of a war against France and Russia seemed plausible to the British public in 1894. In 1895 Britain and Russia came close to war over the Panjdeh Incident, and in 1898 Britain and France were on the verge of war during the Fashoda Incident.
literature.source_title: The Great War in England in 1897

literature.text: In June 1829 the Edinburgh Review published Carlyle's essay Signs of the Times, a decade before Chartism. In it he warned that the Industrial Revolution was turning people into mechanical automatons, and that mechanisation meant both new devices and a mechanistic thought that suppresses human freedom.

The Entente Cordiale of 1904 changed the diplomatic and military landscape, and fiction reflected it. In 1906 Le Queux wrote The Invasion of 1910, in which Germany invades and occupies Britain, stressing the need to prepare for war with Germany. France and Russia became Britain's World War I allies.
literature.source_title: The Great War in England in 1897
tags: The Great War in England in 1897

science.text: Smallpox was a dreaded disease across London, with epidemics in 1816–19, 1825–26, 1837–40, 1871 and 1881. Until the latter part of the century, only a speckling of workhouse hospitals and the London Smallpox Hospital in St Pancras (moved to Highgate Hill in 1848–50) existed to treat its victims.

The Science and Industry Museum in Manchester stands on the site of the world's first inter-urban passenger railway station, Manchester Liverpool Road. The station opened in 1830 as part of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway, and its frontage and 1830 warehouse are Grade I listed.

Unlike in England, industrialization was a late phenomenon in France. In the 1830s France had a limited iron industry and under-developed coal supplies, and most people lived on farms. The systematic establishment of primary education and the creation of new engineering schools prepared an industrial expansion.
science.source_title: France in the long nineteenth century

science.text: The extreme population density of areas like the East End made for unsanitary conditions and epidemics. The most serious disease in the poor quarters was tuberculosis, until the 1860s cholera, as well as rickets, scarlet fever and typhoid. Between 1850 and 1860 the mortality rate from typhoid was 116 per 100,000 people. The child mortality rate in the East End stood at 20%, and the estimated life expectancy of an East End labourer was only 19 years.

The Metropolitan Asylums Board, created in 1867, began building five planned smallpox and fever hospitals to serve different regions of London. They were sited in Stockwell, Deptford, Hampstead, Fulham and Homerton.

Robert Stephenson & Company's Planet class locomotive was constructed in 1830 and hauled trains on the Liverpool and Manchester Railway. A replica was built by the Friends of the Museum of Science and Industry in 1992.

Henri Poincaré (1854–1912) claimed that intuition was the life of mathematics, opposing logicists like Louis Couturat, who believed mathematics was a branch of logic. He held the same view for science, in his book Science and Hypothesis (1902).

Fearful residents succeeded in blocking the building of the Hampstead smallpox hospital, and Fulham residents obtained an injunction preventing all but local cases of smallpox from being treated in theirs. With only three hospitals in operation when the epidemic of 1881 began, the Metropolitan Asylums Board was overwhelmed.

HMS Atlas and Endymion were leased as hospital ships in July 1881, moored at Greenwich. The following year they were purchased along with another, Castalia, and the fleet moved to Long Reach at Gravesend, where it served 20,000 patients between 1884 and 1902.

French rail transport began hesitantly in the 1830s and would not truly develop until the 1840s, using imported British engineers. The industrial worker population of France grew from 23% in 1870 to 39% in 1914.
science.source_title: France in the long nineteenth century

science.text: One of the earliest Rolls-Royce motorcars was built in Hulme, Manchester, in 1905. It is one of three remaining cars of its type and is part of the Science and Industry Museum's collection.

The floating smallpox hospitals had their own river ferry service to transport patients in isolation from the inner city. The ships enabled three permanent isolation hospitals to be built at Dartford, effectively ending the threat of smallpox epidemics.

politics.text: By 1913 the British Empire held sway over 412 million people, which was 23 per cent of the world population at the time. The British Parliament was the supreme law-making authority for all the territories that made up the Empire.

The Act of Union of 1800 formally assimilated Ireland within the British political process. From 1 January 1801 it created a new state called the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the parliament at Westminster became the parliament of the Union.

The French Empire under Napoleon I lasted from 1804 to 1814 and again in 1815, and Napoleon II ruled briefly in 1815. A second French Empire, led by Napoleon III, was the French state from 1852 to 1870.

Britain formally acquired the Dutch Cape Colony in 1806, having occupied it in 1795 to prevent its falling into French hands during the Flanders Campaign. Its Boer population, resentful of British rule, moved north during the Great Trek of the late 1830s and early 1840s to found their own republics.

France gradually absorbed Vietnam's Nguyễn dynasty in the latter half of the 19th century, beginning with the Cochinchina Campaign in 1858. The 1862 Treaty of Saigon made the occupied south the French colony of Cochinchina, and in 1887 Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin and Cambodia were grouped together as French Indochina.
The UK's Slavery Abolition Act 1833 charged the British Royal Navy with ending the global slave trade. The British were the first colonial empire in the century to abolish slavery, doing so in 1834.

The Orange Free State (1854 to 1902) and the South African Republic were the two longer-lived Boer republics. In 1902 Britain occupied both and concluded a treaty with them following the Second Boer War, which ran from 1899 to 1902.

The 1883 Treaty of Huế made the rest of Vietnam into French protectorates, Annam and Tonkin. French diplomatic circles considered its terms overly harsh and it was never ratified in France, so the 1884 Treaty of Huế provided a softened version.

The Cheap Trains Act 1883 helped poorer Londoners relocate by guaranteeing cheap fares and removing a duty imposed on fares since 1844. It led to new working class suburbs including West Ham, Walthamstow, Kilburn and Willesden.

The 1885 Treaty of Tientsin ended the Sino-French War and confirmed Vietnam's status as French protectorates. It severed Vietnam's tributary relationship with the Qing dynasty by requiring that all of Vietnam's foreign affairs be conducted through France.

philosophy.text: John Stuart Mill defended the freedom of the individual against unlimited state control in On Liberty (1859). He continued Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism in works like Utilitarianism (1863), but rejected Bentham's egoism after being influenced by the French philosopher Auguste Comte.

George Boole published The Laws of Thought in 1854, which contains Boolean algebra. Boolean logic is essential to computer programming and is credited with helping to lay the foundations for the Information Age.

Louis-Auguste Blanqui founded Blanquism, which held that socialist revolution should be a coup d'etat by a small group of highly organised and secretive conspirators. He took part in the 1830 Revolution and was a leading voice in the radical clubs of 1848. He spent 33 years of his life in prison, earning the nickname "The Prisoner".

Friedrich Engels wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England after living in Salford and Manchester from 1842 to 1844. He argued that the Industrial Revolution made workers worse off: in industrial cities such as Salford, Manchester and Liverpool, mortality from diseases like smallpox, measles, scarlet fever and whooping cough was four times that of the surrounding countryside, and deaths from convulsions were ten times as high. In Carlisle, 4,408 out of 10,000 children died before age five before the mills arrived (1779–1787), and 4,738 after. When he showed the book to Karl Marx in Paris, it convinced Marx that the working class could be the agent and instrument of the final revolution in history.
philosophy.source_title: The Condition of the Working Class in England
tags: The Condition of the Working Class in England

philosophy.text: Samuel Taylor Coleridge introduced Kant's philosophy and German idealism to Britain in his Biographia Literaria (1817). Thomas Carlyle then introduced many English speakers to German philosophy in his Critical and Miscellaneous Essays (1839), while also parodying German idealism in Sartor Resartus (1834).

Hippolyte Taine, influenced by Cousin and Comte, was a proponent of sociological positivism and historicism. He was deeply shaken by France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 and by the Paris Commune, a revolutionary uprising that was violently suppressed. He then devoted himself to his major historical work, The Origins of Contemporary France (1875-1893).
William Stanley Jevons built a logical machine known as the logic piano. Lewis Carroll wrote a famous paper on logic and infinite regress, "What the Tortoise Said to Achilles" (1895).
tags: What the Tortoise Said to Achilles

philosophy.text: John McTaggart wrote The Unreality of Time (1908), which became seminal in the philosophy of time. He distinguished the tensed A-theory, in which time flows through past, present and future, from the tenseless B-theory of earlier than, simultaneous with and later than.

culture.text: During the 19th and early 20th century, France and in particular Paris was viewed as the capital of Western art and culture. From the late 19th century, France also played an important role in cinema, fashion, cuisine and literature.

France renewed its dominance of high fashion in the years 1860 to 1960 through the great couturier houses, the fashion press and fashion shows. Vogue was founded in 1892 as part of this fashion press.

The birth of Modernism in the late 19th century was centered in Paris and brought innovation to music, dance, architecture and literature. Walter Benjamin called Paris "the capital of the 19th century".

Napoleon and Pope Pius VII signed the Concordat of 1801, which remained in effect until 1905. It aimed at national reconciliation between revolutionaries and Catholics and made the Roman Catholic Church the majority church of France again. Yet the balance of power tilted firmly in Napoleon's favour, since he selected the bishops and supervised church finances.
The first modern Parisian couturier house is generally considered the work of the Englishman Charles Frederick Worth. He dominated the fashion industry from 1858 to 1895.

Haussmann's rebuilt Paris replaced poorer neighborhoods and created fast routes to move troops through the city to quell unrest. Beyond it lay a second Paris on the hill of Montmartre, with its windmills, cabarets and vineyards. Café culture, arcades (19th century covered malls), anarchism and a mixing of classes gave the city a stunning vibrancy.

The Concordat of 1801 was an agreement between Napoleon and Pope Pius VII that remained in effect until 1905. It restored much of the Roman Catholic Church's civil status in France, but Napoleon selected the bishops and supervised church finances.
London's Highgate Cemetery, opened in 1839, drew on Egyptian veneration of the dead and beliefs about the afterlife. Its themed features included a 'Gothic Catacomb' as well as an 'Egyptian Avenue'.
culture.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

culture.text: From 1880 to 1890 lay women replaced nuns in many French hospitals. In 1879 priests were excluded from hospital administrative committees, and in 1881 the government cut off salaries to priests it disliked, though Napoleon's 1801 Concordat stayed in operation.

During the Dreyfus Affair (1894–1906), Catholics were for the most part anti-Dreyfusard. The Assumptionists published antisemitic and anti-republican articles in their journal La Croix, which infuriated republican politicians.

In 1892 Pope Leo XIII issued an encyclical advising French Catholics to rally to the Republic and defend the Church by taking part in republican politics. The attempt to improve relations failed, and suspicions on both sides were inflamed by the Dreyfus Affair.

In 1884, Pope Leo XIII told French bishops not to act in a hostile manner toward the State. In 1892 he advised French Catholics to rally to the Republic and defend the Church through republican politics. The attempt failed, as suspicions on both sides were inflamed by the Dreyfus Affair.

Chaplains were removed from naval and military hospitals in 1903 and 1904, and soldiers were ordered not to frequent Catholic clubs in 1904. These measures came as the Waldeck-Rousseau and Combes Ministries fought with the Vatican over the appointment of bishops.
